articles.title: Unsafe blood transfusions
articles.content: “BLOOD transfusions (48pc) and contaminated needle use (48pc) are the primary contributors to the outbreak.” This was the conclusion of a joint mission by the Punjab government, WHO, Unicef and UNAIDS investigating the HIV outbreak among children in Taunsa, Dera Ghazi Khan. Between Dec 2024 and April 2025, 120 children under 12 were infected. As unsafe practices continued, the number eventually reached 331, by the time the BBC made its incriminating documentary. How many more outbreaks will it take before we recognise that this is not an isolated medical mishap but a systemic governance failure? Pakistan has one of the fastest-growing HIV epidemics in Asia and the world’s largest burden of hepatitis C. Both are blood-borne infections. Unsafe transfusions and contaminated injections are preventable sources of infection, yet they continue to endanger lives, particularly those of poor children who depend on an inadequately regulated healthcare system. Unsafe blood flows through non-functional institutions. The tragedy is not that Pakistan lacks the knowledge to make blood transfusions safe. It is that we repeatedly fail to translate policies, technical knowledge and institutional arrangements into action. Consider history. Established in 2010 with substantial German financial and technical assistance, the Safe Blood Transfusion Programme (SBTP) made important progress. It established 17 state-of-the-art Regional Blood Centres (RBCs) and upgraded and linked 83 public-sector hospital blood banks. It also supported relevant policies, legislation, technical guidelines, training and monitoring systems. Yet the programme gradually became dormant. After its national coordinator retired in 2020, no replacement was appointed, to date. The programme lost momentum, and opportunities to sustain international cooperation were not adequately pursued. A national initiative that had laid the foundations of reform was left high and dry, without the leadership needed to carry it forward. This is a familiar Pakistani story: programmes are launched, institutions established, laws enacted and policies approved. Then positions remain vacant, resources are withheld, regulations unfinished and accountability absent. The consequences are visible nationwide. Islamabad’s Blood Transfusion Authority is non-functional, while its RBC remained inoperative for years before being handed over to the Indus Hospital & Health Network in July 2026. Punjab has yet to frame rules under its 2016 law. Sindh has failed to replace outdated rules despite subsequent legislation. Khyber Pakhtunkhwa has a regulatory framework, but its regional centres remain underutilised. Balochistan has laws and institutions, but lacks adequate operational capacity, staffing and financing. In Aug 2026, a Technical Working Group (TWG) was established following the prime minister’s intervention after the Taunsa outbreak. Its mandate is to translate the earlier task force’s recommendations into action, also reflected in the National Blood Transfusion and Blood Products Policy 2025-2030. The TWG reports directly to the PM monthly. The TWG’s Sept 2026 policy brief provides a practical roadmap. Its value lies not in announcing another policy but in specifying actions that must be implemented immediately. First, the SBTP must be revived, with a merit-based, qualified national coordinator, professional staff, a functioning office and adequate resources. The centre must ensure sustainable financing through the recurrent budget and seek renewed international cooperation. Second, regulatory authorities must become functional. Islamabad needs an operational authority with competent staff and adequate funding. Punjab must frame rules under its existing law and strengthen its authority. Sindh must finalise regulations and build institutional capacity. KP and Balochistan need effective provincial counterparts to the national programme. Third, RBCs must be linked to hospital blood banks across the public and private sectors. Existing centres are underutilised. Connecting more hospitals would expand access to quality-assured blood and reduce fragmentation. Blood safety cannot be confined to government hospitals while private establishments escape effective regulation. Fourth, screening standards must be enforced uniformly. The TWG recommends automated chemiluminescence immunoassay as the minimum screening standard, with nucleic acid testing introduced as an additional safeguard. Manual rapid diagnostic kits must be prohibited for donor screening. A real-time national database, including a donor deferral registry, should prevent people with reactive screening results from donating blood again. Fifth, the Inter-Ministerial Health and Population Council should regularly review blood safety and monitor implementation. Model regulations should be approved by the National Technical Advisory Committee and adopted by provincial authorities. Finally, Pakistan should reduce its dependence on imported plasma-derived medicinal products. While these products are imported at considerable cost, recovered plasma is wasted or discarded. The TWG recommends a national plasma fractionation programme, with WHO technical assistance, to improve availability and move towards domestic production. The roadmap is clear. What remains uncertain is whether political will, administrative discipline and financial commitment will be sustained long enough to implement it. The PM’s direct involvement offers an opportunity, but personal intervention cannot substitute for strong institutions. The real test is whether competent professionals are appointed, funds released, regulations enforced, hospitals connected to safe blood supplies and results independently monitored. Nor can governments act alone. Citizens, professional associations, medical practitioners, civil society and the media must demand safe healthcare and hold public and private providers accountable. Voluntary, non-remunerated blood donation must be encouraged while infection prevention and control guidelines must be implemented. The children of Taunsa have already paid an unacceptable price for our collective failure. Their suffering must not become another forgotten episode in Pakistan’s public health history. The choice is stark: continue treating each outbreak as a temporary media scandal, or confront the institutional weaknesses that make the next one possible. Unsafe blood flows through non-functional institutions. The writer is a former SAPM on health with ministerial status, adjunct professor of health systems and president of the Pakistan Association of Lifestyle Medicine.
articles.author: Zafar Mirza

articles.title: Quintessential capitalism
articles.content: FEW companies are hailed as proof of free-market genius more than Tesla. Yet, at every turn that mattered, it stood on public capital. In 2010 it borrowed $465m from a US federal programme open to every carmaker building cleaner vehicles, in a country where transport is now the largest source of greenhouse gases. It paid the Treasury’s own cost, roughly one to 3.4 per cent, with principal deferred until production began. One of the smallest borrowers, it became the star, repaying with interest nine years early. Regulatory credits, earned by beating emission rules and bought by those that fall short, then carried it into profit. Pakistan asks its banks to do alone what no quintessential capitalist economy asks of its own: lend to priority sectors without the state sharing the risk and the price. This is not a lesson taken from state-led economies such as China, where public support is part of the model. It comes from the market economies themselves, which do it openly and without apology. Tesla is not their exception; it is their method. Look at where they aim interest subsidies, and how deep. Farming comes first: America lends beginning farmers money to buy land at under 2pc and caps their operating microloans at 5pc, while Canada pays the interest on the first C$250,000 of each grower’s cash advance. Housing is next: France gives first-time buyers zero-interest loans and compensates banks through tax credits. Then enterprise: Britain lends start-ups unsecured at a fixed 6pc, with mentoring, and its firms outlive their peers; Germany’s KfW cheapens founders’ loans and absorbs four-fifths of any loss so local banks will lend. In every case, the taxpayer took the first risk and part of the financing cost, at the stage private finance would not, and demanded performance in return. And the subsidy went to the borrower, the priority-sector player, not the lender: the bank is paid only the market interest the borrower is spared. Subsidies have built giants, and an emerging economy needs them more, not less. That is the global norm. Why, then, is Pakistan so averse to it? Here, subsidy for producers is treated as a dirty word, subsidised credit is misread as a benefit to banks, and lenders are blamed for holding back from risks their peers abroad never shoulder unaided. Asking them to match the world’s lending without the world’s toolkit is neither fair nor realistic. The money exists; its direction is the problem. This year’sfederal budgetallocates Rs838bn to the Benazir Income Support Programme, up by a sixth, and almost as much to the power sector; provincial budgets add their own spending on wheat, fertiliser and household relief. Little of it is designed to make the poor bankable. BISP is indispensable.Reaching some 10 million familiesthrough a national registry and digital payments, it is one of the country’s institutional achievements, and that safety net must stay. But a stipend, by its nature, protects rather than transforms. A net that never becomes a springboard keeps the poor safe, but poor. BISP must now be balanced with wealth creation at the lower strata of society, so that families able to work have a path from support to enterprise. Wealth, like subsidy, is not a bad word. It can be created at every level, including the bottom, and it is what keeps incomes rising sustainably. The cliché about wealth must go, just like subsidies. So add a ramp without lowering the floor: dedicate a tenth of BISP’s allocation to an enterprise window within the programme; that is smaller than this year’s increase, so no family need receive less than last year. Run it as the world does. Target precisely: older people, persons with disabilities and households with no working member keep their full stipend; working-age households, starting with the women BISP serves, get concessional credit for livestock, horticulture, cottage industry, solar trades and digital work. Price it for the borrower: the first loan interest-free and repeat loans at no more than 5pc, the state paying the difference. Pay for delivery: lenders earn the subsidy only for verified results, and every loan comes with training and a mentor. Build the exit: the stipend tapers only once the business stands, and the subsidy steps down with each cycle. Even at today’s rates, that tenth could carry some Rs400bn of lending: over a million small businesses. Audit it independently after three years; scale it only if it works. Two objections deserve answers. Credit alone, global trials show, raises poor families’ incomes only modestly; what lifts them for good is capital paired with training and continued support while the business finds its feet, which is this design. Nor does the window raid BISP: it is paid for from the programme’s growth and serves the same households. It is time to retire the reflex that subsidies never create wealth or welfare. Bad design is bad; subsidy is not, if it pays for the initial risk rather than permanent inefficiency. Subsidies have built giants, and an emerging economy needs them more, not less. Washington’s decisive bet on Tesla was not a stipend but a loan, tied to milestones. Pakistan’s Teslas are smaller — a woman’s dairy herd, a tailor’s workshop, a graduate’s laptop — but they deserve the same deal: capital to start, conditions to keep, and a way out. Then the cycle begins again with the next borrower. That is routine in every quintessential capitalist economy, and it should be in Pakistan too. The writer is a development-focused and impact-oriented banker.
articles.author: Zafar Masud

articles.title: What a child drinks
articles.content: AT the recent Act for Nutrition Conference in Islamabad, organised by DawnMedia, where I joined a panel examining the link between poor water, sanitation and child stunting, much of the discussion was rightly about food: what children eat, how mothers are supported, and why so many families still struggle to access a nutritious diet. But sitting on that panel, I kept returning to another part of the stunting story that receives far less attention: what is the child drinking? What happens when the water available at home is unsafe, sanitation is poor, or repeated diarrhoea becomes part of a child’s earliest years? A child can be fed and still struggle to grow. Pakistan’s water figures make this difficult to ignore. According to the WHO/Unicef Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP, 2025), 91 per cent of Pakistan’s population used at least basic drinking-water services in 2024, but only 45pc used safely managed drinking-water services. That distinction matters. Safely managed water comes from an improved source that is on the premises, available when needed and free from contamination. A water source may therefore be available without the water necessarily being safe. This is particularly important during the first 1,000 days of a child’s life. Good food, breastfeeding and maternal nutrition are essential. But so is the environment in which a child is growing. Repeated exposure to contaminated water and poor sanitation can mean repeated illness at precisely the stage when healthy growth matters most. Yet our response is still organised in separate boxes. Nutrition has its programmes. Health has another set of structures. Water and sanitation are often treated as infrastructure. Social protection and climate sit elsewhere. Children do not experience those divisions. They experience the water available at home, the food they are given, where they play and how often they fall sick. Our work in rural Punjab has made this very clear. Through the Behaviour Change and Capacity Development project, WaterAid Pakistan led a consortium, working with the Punjab Rural Municipal Services Company across 200 villages. The work began not by assuming that people simply needed more information, but by looking at what they were already doing and why. How was drinking water stored? When were hands washed? How was food prepared? Where did child and animal faeces go? What made a safer practice easy to adopt, and what made it difficult? That research informed a Hygiene Behaviour Change Package covering safe water, handwashing, food hygiene, sanitation, breastfeeding, vaccination, menstrual hygiene and household and animal waste. Families were engaged repeatedly through community sessions, practical activities, visual materials, videos and behavioural cues. Our evaluation covered 1,072 households, alongside focus groups, interviews and household observations. Ninety-eight per cent of surveyed households reported adopting new hygiene-related behaviours, 89pc reported washing their hands with soap at critical times, and 86pc reported safe drinking-water use and storage practices. These figures do not mean behaviour change is the answer to stunting. Nor does one project offer a solution to a national problem. But they do show why infrastructure and behaviour cannot be treated separately. There is little point in asking a family to use safe water when safe water is not available. But installing a water system does not automatically change how water is stored, how hands are washed or how waste is managed. The approach and communication materials tested in Punjab now form part of PRMSC’s planned expansion to another 1,800 villages. That is important because Pakistan does not lack pilots. The harder task is getting useful evidence into public systems and taking what works to scale. The same thinking should shape our nutrition response. When a programme identifies a child at risk of stunting, safe water and sanitation at home should be part of that picture. When a child is treated for diarrhoea, the conditions they return to matter. And when money is being spent on nutrition, health, water or social protection, those investments should work together. WASH is not the only answer to malnutrition. Food insecurity, poverty, maternal health and access to healthcare remain central. But what a child eats is only part of the story. If we want children to grow well, we also need to pay attention to what they drink and the environment in which they spend their earliest years. The writer is Country Director, WaterAid Pakistan.
articles.author: Mian Muhammad Junaid

articles.title: Nuclear jingoism
articles.content: INDIA’S nuclear jingoism was on ample display duringOperation Marka-i-Haqin May 2025 when it fired dual-use BrahMos cruise missiles with conventional payload, unmindful of the fact that the dangerous caper could have been misconstrued by Pakistani air defenders as a nuclear attack. Despite an agreement on pre-notification of flight testing of ballistic missiles, the Indians, while testing the Agni V MIRV-capable missile, have shown a blithe disregard for established pre-notification protocols that mandate a 72-hour pre-test notification, a fact pointed out by Pakistan’s Foreign Office in 2024. While the Indians keep up an implacable momentum of vertical proliferation of nuclear and missile technology, the world indulges them through exceptionalism enshrined in the nuclear waiver for the Nuclear Suppliers Group and membership of the Missile Technology Control Regime. The Indians have slyly wangled the concession from the USA and IAEA in the civil nuclear deal to keep eight reactors out of IAEA oversight. These pressurised heavy water reactors consume less nuclear fuel than they produce, which can be harvested for strategic military purposes. It should be remembered that it was the Indians who introduced the nuclear arms race in the subcontinent because of their grandiose big-power pretensions. Their nuclear explosions in 1974 and 1998 forced Pakistan tofollow suitout of its security compulsions. The world indulges India through nuclear exceptionalism. The Indian nuclear security architecture was provided conceptual ballast by Gen K. Sunderji and Krishna Subramanyam in the 1980s, when they came up with the notion of no-first use of nuclear weapons against a non-nuclear nation, with a caveat of making an exception for biological and chemical attacks. However, India kept developing its conventional forces, especially the armoured and mechanised component, as per the Sunderji doctrine, aimed at tearing Pakistan asunder. On the geopolitical level the Indians have acquiesced to the status of a regional surrogate to accommodate balancing needs of the US vis-a-vis a rising global competitor, China. While enjoying nuclear exceptionalism the Indians went on a shopping spree for nuclear technology as well as the conventional hardware to operationalise the military strategy that sought an elusive space for conventional wars under the nuclear overhang. The operational manifestation of these military ambitions was a slew of concepts starting with Cold Start and graduating to proactive operations. The latest manifestation of those concepts is the Dynamic Response Strategy that is based on rapidly deployable all-arms-based integrated battle groups and multidomain-enabled terrain-customised brigade-sized groups called Rudra Brigades. Pakistan relies on its full-spectrum deterrence, keeping strategic nuclear ambiguity for greater liberty of action to deny India the space for conventional conflict. While India deploys non-state actors to keep Pakistan destabilised through terrorism, it cleverly conflates Pakistan’s principled support to the victims of Indian state repression in Occupied Kashmir, a UNSC-recognised dispute, with militancy. It has also withdrawn from its international law commitments byillegally holding the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyanceand imperilling the food security of Pakistan. India under the BJP and RSS sway has adopted a foreign policy based upon the antiquated notion of ‘Akhand Bharat’ that covets the territories of neighbours based on historical myths. The inflammatory statement of Prime Minister Narendra Modi at Barmer, Rajasthan, during an election rally that “Indian nukes are not kept for Diwali” indicates a bellicose mindset. It is against the backdrop of the above facts that the notions of nuclear deterrence in the subcontinent have to be understood. Since the stability of nuclear deterrence is based upon nuclear dialectics between two rational actors, Indian irrationality adds dangerous instability to the nuclear equation. The deployment of canisterised ground-based ready-to-use nuclear missiles and the submarine-launched nuclear ballistic missiles point to an aggressive nuclear intent when viewed in the context of Indo-Pak distrust and irrationality of the ideologically driven BJP leadership. The well-known military historian Martin Van Creveld had coined a term for wars in the nuclear era: “Non-trinitarian”, where, unlike Clausewitz’s trinitarian wars, the only political objective would be deterring and not winning the wars. Whether India has strengthened or reduced its strategic deterrence by fielding shallow-range submarine-based missiles is a point to ponder by Indian nuclear strategists.
articles.author: Dr Raashid Wali Janjua

articles.title: Candid admission
articles.content: PARLIAMENT has recently been debating the future of Pakistani democracy, but those debates will be for naught unless our leaders also develop the capacity to acknowledge each other’s positions. The past two days have seen the government and opposition benches trading blame for democracy’s present, rather sorry state. On Wednesday, JUI-F chief Maulana Fazlur Rehmanaccusedthe government of misusing the Constitution and resorting to unconstitutional measures. He also said his party was “prepared to die” resisting the government if the latter continued pursuing a policy of confrontation and violence, and proposed a new Charter of Democracy as the way out. Regretting that hisefforts to mediatebetween the government and the PTI had failed because the government had changed course andimposedan emergency and governor’s rule in KP, the maulana said the political leadership had grown too intolerant for parliament to do its job. He was not wrong, though the fault is hardly the government’s alone. The maulana’s rebuke drew two kinds of response. Minister of Defence Khawaja Asifresorted to personal attacks, insinuating that the JUI-F chief was merely sore at being denied a share of power in KP. PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari, on the other hand, was more circumspect. Though he, too, laid much of the blame for parliament’s dysfunction on the opposition, he nonethelessurgedit to exercise its powers and return to parliamentary committees. “Those who want this House to remain dysfunctional and do not want the people of Pakistan to benefit from it have succeeded,” he told the opposition benches. “You have played a part in helping these people achieve their objective.” It was a surprisingly candid admission that the House’s dysfunction serves interests other than the people’s, even if the PPP chief left out his own party’s role in getting us here. They may have yet to come to terms with it, but both ruling and opposition parties have lost credibility and political ground due to their ongoing vendetta. The maulana’s call for a new Charter of Democracy, though welcome, looks difficult to realise when the two sides cannot even agree to sit together in parliamentary committees. The imposition of emergency and governor’s rule in KP was a gross misstep by the federal government, and it has spoiled the chances of a negotiated settlement. But the opposition, too, has gained little from confrontation. Unless both sides start to show some flexibility on key matters, make compromises and enter negotiations without preconditions, they risk further deepening this crisis of their own making. If enough lawmakers on both sides of the aisle are willing to admit that matters have gone too far, there may yet be hope for parliament, and for Pakistani democracy. The question is, are they ready to do so?
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Disrupted LPG supply
articles.content: THE petroleum minister’s explanation in the National Assembly that the recent closure of the Iran border has disrupted liquefied petroleum gas supplies and driven up prices identifies a major cause of the current crisis. The subsequent partial border reopening has failed to ease the shortage. While the closure may have triggered the present shortages and price hike, the problem recurs every winter. Pakistan produces only about a quarter of the LPG it needs. The rest is imported, mainly from Iran. The disruption of cross-border trade has therefore exposed the vulnerability of a market that depends heavily on external supplies. The Iran war has also complicated efforts to bring in more by sea. The minister says efforts are being made to increase seaborne supplies, but consumers have yet to see relief. The state must explain what additional volumes have been secured, and when they will arrive. Further, why were no contingency measures taken before the Iran border closure, especially when the authorities knew that the onset of winter would push up demand? The decision-makers owe an explanation to people suffering due to sudden shortages and price shock. That said, the current LPG supply disruption is only part of the wider story. LPG prices have historically surged as winter approaches, even without a major supply shock. This recurring pattern suggests that the crisis is not simply the result of border closure. Inadequate advance planning, weak market oversight and the failure to build reliable supply arrangements leave consumers exposed whenever demand rises or imports are interrupted. The consequences are particularly harsh for households without access to piped natural gas. Millions of families in northern Pakistan, remote and hilly areas, and parts of Punjab depend on LPG for cooking and, during colder months, heating. Low gas pressure and restricted supplies in connected areas also push more consumers towards cylinders, adding to demand. With the official price around Rs280 per kg and reported market rates reaching Rs500-800, an essential fuel has become unaffordable for many. Blaming the Iran border closure is but an attempt to cover up the ministry’s failure to do its basic duty: ensure adequate supplies ahead of the closure and enforce the official fuel price.
articles.author: Editorial
